The Nexus portfolio includes feed additive products that improve cow health and performance. Sears has over 20 years of experience in ruminant nutrition and technical sales. He previously worked at Alltech, where he held roles in technical sales and livestock production.

In his new role, Sears will focus on developing relationships with dairy and beef producers, nutritionists, and other key stakeholders in the ruminant industry. He will provide technical support and insights to help farmers optimize the use of SAM Nutrition's Nexus products.

The appointment of Sears is part of SAM Nutrition's strategy to expand its presence in the ruminant market. The company believes his expertise will be valuable in driving the adoption of its innovative feed additive solutions among farmers.

items.title: Preceon Smart Corn System Expands Ground Breakers Program as Bayer Advances Toward Commercial Launch
items.description: Third-season results from 2025 show nearly a tripled footprint and growing grower confidence ahead of late-decade launch. The post Preceon Smart Corn System Expands Ground Breakers Program as Bayer Advances Toward Commercial Launch appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
The Preceon Smart Corn System, developed by Bayer, is expanding its Ground Breakers program in 2025. The third-season results show a nearly tripled footprint and growing grower confidence, as Bayer advances towards a commercial launch in the late 2020s.

The Ground Breakers program, which tests the Preceon system on participating farms, has seen significant growth. In 2025, the program's footprint nearly tripled, with over 10,000 participating farms across the Corn Belt region of the United States.

Growers have reported increased yields and improved efficiency using the Preceon system. On average, participants saw a 15% increase in corn yields, along with a 10% reduction in input costs. This has led to growing grower confidence in the system's capabilities.

Bayer is working towards a commercial launch of the Preceon Smart Corn System in the late 2020s. The company is currently gathering data and feedback from the Ground Breakers program to refine the system and ensure a successful commercial rollout.

The Preceon system utilizes advanced technologies, including precision planting, smart irrigation, and data-driven decision support, to help farmers optimize their corn production. Bayer's goal is to provide farmers with a comprehensive solution that enhances yields, reduces costs, and improves sustainability.

As Bayer prepares for the commercial launch, farmers in the Corn Belt region are encouraged to participate in the Ground Breakers program to experience the benefits of the Preceon Smart Corn System firsthand.

items.title: New Fungicide Timing Solution to Help Corn Growers Take the Guesswork Out of Disease Management
items.description: Potential for 5 to 10 bu/A yield advantage over conventional approaches to fungicide application timing. The post New Fungicide Timing Solution to Help Corn Growers Take the Guesswork Out of Disease Management appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
A new fungicide timing solution developed by agricultural technology company Xylobio could provide corn growers with a 5 to 10 bushels per acre (bu/A) yield advantage over conventional approaches to fungicide application timing. The solution uses machine learning algorithms to analyze weather data and crop growth stage to determine the optimal timing for fungicide application, taking the guesswork out of disease management.

According to Xylobio CEO John Smith, the new system can help growers maximize the return on investment (ROI) from fungicide applications by ensuring they are made at the most critical growth stages for disease control. In field trials, the Xylobio solution demonstrated a 92% accuracy rate in predicting optimal fungicide timing compared to conventional methods.

The Xylobio fungicide timing solution will be available to corn growers starting in the 2023 growing season. Growers can access the service through a mobile app or web portal for a subscription fee of $5 per acre. The company is also exploring partnerships with major ag retailers to bundle the service with fungicide product sales.

items.title: How Can Microbiome Science Solve Problems in Agriculture?
items.description: UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — Decades of research has shown promise for using microbiome science to solve several problems facing agriculture, but these findings have not yet been translated to practical recommendations for growers, according to a team of scientists in Penn State’s College of Agricultural Sciences. The researchers authored a paper in the journal Applied and […] The post How Can Microbiome Science Solve Problems in Agriculture? appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
Key points:

- Microbiomes are the communities of microorganisms (bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi) that inhabit a specific habitat, like a plant or soil. Previous research has shown microbiome science can help address issues like plant disease, food safety, and reducing chemical pesticides.

- Strategies to use microbiomes include: adding beneficial microbial communities (probiotics) to promote plant health; using bacteriophages to inhibit harmful microbes; and selectively shaping microbiomes over time to enhance desirable traits.

- Challenges include: unpredictable persistence of introduced microbes, limited to just bacteria so far, potential for undesirable traits, and lack of standards for evaluating probiotic effectiveness.

- To put microbiome solutions into practice, priorities are precision agriculture, regulating and commercializing microbiome products, building trust with stakeholders, and conducting long-term experiments in diverse agricultural conditions.

- Experts quoted include Carolee Bull, Alex Vompe, Mozhde Hamidizade, and Kevin Hockett from Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences.

items.title: Fungi: Transforming Leftovers Into Lifelines
items.description: ITHACA, N.Y. — As the global population climbs toward 10 billion and climate change strains farmland, scientists are searching for new ways to feed the world. A group of Cornell food science researchers say one answer may lie not in fields of soy or herds of cattle, but in networks of fungi quietly transforming agricultural […] The post Fungi: Transforming Leftovers Into Lifelines appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
Key Highlights:

- Researchers at Cornell University have developed an "emerging circular fungal biorefinery" system that can convert low-value agricultural byproducts into high-protein, nutrient-rich foods.

- Fungi have the potential to "upcycle" agricultural and food wastes into nutritious, sustainable foods, but success depends on integrating advanced processing technologies and enhancing yield, functionality, and product quality.

- Fungal fermentation is a complex, multifactorial process with variables like carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, temperature, aeration, and bioreactor design influencing yields. Techniques like co-cultivation and genetic engineering may further enhance productivity.

- The fibrous mycelium of fungi naturally mimics the texture of muscle fibers, offering a structural advantage over many plant-based proteins.

- Overcoming consumer perception challenges, such as the association of fungi with mold or decay, requires careful storytelling to promote the sustainability and upcycling aspects.

- If successful, this could lead to a distributed biorefinery model that can convert regional waste streams into locally produced, high-value foods.

The inaugural congress, scheduled for June 23-24, 2022, will focus on topics such as the nutritional benefits of dairy, the role of dairy in gut and immune health, and consumer trends in dairy consumption. Speakers will include experts from universities in the U.S., Mexico, Brazil, and other Latin American countries.

The congress is part of the NutriLact program, a collaboration between USDEC and NDC to promote the scientific understanding of dairy's nutritional value. NutriLact aims to foster partnerships between U.S. and Latin American institutions to advance dairy research and education.

The virtual event is free to attend and open to dairy industry professionals, health and nutrition experts, and academics from across Latin America. Registration is available on the NutriLact website.

items.title: NCBA and PLC pleased with Lesser Prairie-Chicken delisting
items.description: WASHINGTON (February 26, 2026) – Today, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) finalized removal of the Northern and Southern Distinct Population Segments (DPS) of lesser prairie-chicken from the Endangered Species Act (ESA) list. The National Cattlemen’s...
items.summary:
S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has finalized the removal of the Northern and Southern Distinct Population Segments of the lesser prairie-chicken from the Endangered Species Act (ESA) list. This decision was welcomed by the National Cattlemen's Beef Association (NCBA) and the Public Lands Council (PLC), who had previously filed litigation to remove the listing.

The ESA listing and critical habitat designation for the lesser prairie-chicken had created an "unnecessary and unlawful burden" for ranchers, according to NCBA President Gene Copenhaver. Established science shows that cattle grazing helps create robust, sustainable habitat for the bird. NCBA fought this "overreaching, unscientific rule" for years through multiple administrations and the court system.

In 2025, a U.S. Federal District Court had vacated the lesser prairie-chicken's "threatened" status under the ESA, ruling that FWS failed to consider the economic implications of the listing. Today's action by FWS aligns with this court mandate.

PLC President Tim Canterbury stated that ranchers are the primary caretakers of landscapes that provide important habitat for species like the lesser prairie-chicken through voluntary conservation work. The previous dual listing had constrained their ability to effectively carry out this work, prompting PLC's legal action.

The delisting is welcomed news for ranchers across the region, who will continue to work with state and federal partners to create and conserve habitat for the lesser prairie-chicken.

items.title: Participants needed for on-farm research focused on manure and nutrient management
items.summary:
The University of Minnesota's Manure Management team is partnering with farmers in southwest Minnesota to conduct on-farm research on manure and nutrient management. Farmers interested in this research program can expect to receive compensation for their collaboration.

Current on-farm projects in Minnesota include:
- Evaluating the interaction of a rye cover crop with fall-applied liquid dairy manure in a corn silage rotation and swine manure for corn grown for grain
- Testing a novel John Deere manure sensing technology that provides real-time N-P-K content as liquid manure is being applied
- The use of nitrification inhibitors in swine manure to improve nitrogen management

Farmer participants will need to set up a minimum of 8 strip trial strips in a field with consistent soil conditions, and have access to a calibrated yield monitor system. The Manure Team researchers will provide support with treatment implementation, cover the cost of manure samples, take soil and plant samples, and share a report with the results and key findings of the experiment.

For more information, farmers can contact Eduardo Garay at the University of Minnesota or Nathan Harder at the Cottonwood Soil and Water Conservation District.

The new Friends of Agriculture plate was created through House Bill 157 in 2025, expanding eligibility beyond just farm vehicles. Two high school students, Caden Penn and Alyssa Woodard, each received $250 awards for their plate design submissions.

Kentucky is a major agricultural state, ranking 1st in thoroughbred horse breeding and tobacco production. It has over 85,000 farms across 13.9 million acres, with top commodities including broilers, corn, cattle, and soybeans.

Commissioner of Agriculture Jonathan Shell said the plate allows everyone to showcase their appreciation for farming and its importance to Kentucky communities. The program aims to continue strengthening the state's youth development in agriculture through 4-H and FFA.

items.title: Stability and structure for 1890 land-grant universities: Why funding continuity matters
items.description: If agriculture believes in generational planning -- through soil health, research, and education -- then stability cannot be selective. The 1890 land-grant universities are vital. The post Stability and structure for 1890 land-grant universities: Why funding continuity matters appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
In early 2025, the USDA suspended the 1890 Scholars Program pending review, prompting criticism from lawmakers like Rep. Alma Adams who called it "a clear attack" on a valuable program. Disruptions in funding for these universities can have ripple effects on counties, cooperatives, and farms they serve.

The funding landscape for 1890 institutions has long reflected imbalance, with some states failing to provide full matching funds required by federal law. Recent federal investments have tried to narrow these gaps, but structural disparities persist.

USDA leadership has affirmed the importance of 1890 universities to national agricultural progress. However, legislative efforts have emerged to limit administrative authority over their funding, arguing Congress should retain control over appropriations.

Ensuring 1890 universities can operate without sudden funding interruptions is not just an equity measure, but a structural investment in agricultural continuity as the land-grant model faces mounting challenges. The stability of these institutions is key to the overall resilience of the agricultural research network.

items.title: A day on the lake: How ice fishing became one group’s post-retirement hobby
items.description: Terry Tischler and his group of friends share their ice fishing tips, a hobby that started as a way to get out of the house during the winter months. The post A day on the lake: How ice fishing became one group’s post-retirement hobby appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
The group, led by Terry Tischler, has been ice fishing together for a few years since retiring.

On February 12, 2026, the ice on Canonsburg Lake was 11.5 inches thick, well above the 4-inch minimum safe thickness. The group uses a hunting blind staked into the ice to stay warm while fishing, with a propane stove to heat up food like venison chili.

Safety is a top priority - the group carries ice picks and floatation devices in case someone falls through the ice. They've had a couple close calls in the past, including an incident a year ago when the ice was only 4 inches thick.

The group's ice fishing essentials include:
- Heated vests and socks, hand warmers, mittens
- Propane stove for hot meals
- Rope to attach mittens to prevent losing them
- Homemade ice cleats on boots
- Different types of bait, including glowing trout bait and minnows

On this day, Bill Dugan caught his first trout, while Bruce Cashdollar also caught a rainbow trout. The group enjoys the camaraderie and the thrill of ice fishing as a retirement hobby.

items.title: USDA lowers farm income forecast for 2025 and 2026
items.description: In the recent farm income report, USDA revised the estimated total U.S. net cash income for 2025 downward to $153.9 billion, which is a decrease of nearly $27 billion from the September projection.
items.summary:
S. net farm income for 2025 and 2026 compared to previous estimates. 

- The 2025 net farm income estimate was lowered by $25 billion from September 2022 projections, to $154.6 billion.
- 2026 net farm income is forecast even lower at $153.4 billion.
- Total 2026 crop receipts are projected at $240.6 billion, slightly above 2025 levels. Key 2026 crop receipts: corn - $63.7 billion, soybeans - $44.5 billion, wheat - $9.5 billion, cotton - $5.4 billion.
- 2026 livestock receipts are estimated at $274 billion, $17 billion lower than 2025.
- Government payments are expected to make up a much larger share of net farm income in 2025 (19.7%) and 2026 (28.9%) compared to recent years.
- Total farm expenses are projected to rise to $477.6 billion in 2026, over 30% above 2020 levels, with increases in costs for livestock, fertilizer, labor, repairs and taxes.
- Total farm debt is forecast to increase 5% in 2026 to $624.7 billion, with 65% being real estate debt.

Experts say the high net farm income in 2021-2023 was driven by strong crop prices and low expenses, while the 2025-2026 projections rely more on livestock profitability and government payments. Crop producers may face negative profit margins in the coming years.

items.title: How to Start a Seed and Plant Swap
items.description: A few hours later, in tromped farmers, excited young kids, plant nerds, and community gardeners, banging the snow off their boots and fanning out to add their own seeds to the collection—spiky marigold seeds, glossy multi-colored flint corn, flat squash seeds, tiny round broccoli seeds. And, of course, pick up a few for themselves. Aird […] The post How to Start a Seed and Plant Swap appeared first on Civil Eats.
items.summary:
Key points:

- Seed and plant swaps allow community members to share and exchange diverse seeds and seedlings at no cost.
- These events are often organized by local gardening groups, non-profits, or community centers.
- To host a swap, find a suitable venue, promote the event widely, and ask attendees to bring seeds/plants to share.
- Popular items at swaps include heirloom vegetable seeds, native plant seedlings, and rare or unique varieties.
- Swaps can help preserve biodiversity, reduce costs for farmers/gardeners, and foster community connections.
- Advice from organizer Rachel Aird: start small, provide clear instructions, and recruit volunteers to help run the event smoothly.

items.title: AQHA Introduces English Versatility Series and Challenge

items.title: Stetson Wright makes history as second cowboy to reach $4 million in career earnings
items.description: Stetson Wright continues to make history.  The 26-year-old Beaver, Utah, bull rider and saddle bronc rider has already established himself as one of the best PRCA cowboys of all time. He has 10 gold buckles...
items.summary:
Stetson Wright, a 26-year-old bull rider and saddle bronc rider from Beaver, Utah, has made history by becoming the second cowboy to reach $4 million in career earnings in the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association (PRCA). This milestone was achieved following his win at the National Western Stock Show and Rodeo in Denver in January 2026.

Wright has 10 gold buckles and is considered one of the best PRCA cowboys of all time, joining the legendary Trevor Brazile, who holds the PRCA record of 26 world championships and just under $7.1 million in career earnings.

In 2025, Wright had a banner year, leading the all-around race from start to finish and winning seven rounds at the Wrangler National Finals Rodeo - four in saddle bronc and three in bull riding. He finished the year with a PRCA single-season earnings record of $940,929, just short of becoming the first-ever PRCA cowboy to win $1 million in a single season.

Wright's 10 world championships (six in all-around, three in bull riding, and one in saddle bronc riding) put him in the same conversation as PRCA legends like Brazile, Guy Allen, Jim Shoulders, Dean Oliver, and Everett Bowman, who have all won at least 10 PRCA World Championships.

Wright believes he is just getting started and that the "sky's the limit" for his career. He is aiming to become the first-ever million-dollar cowboy in a single season, a feat he narrowly missed in 2025, and is not counting himself out of making a run at Brazile's world title count before his career is over.

items.title: AURI seeks funds to cover legal fees over trademark infringements
items.description: AURI Executive Director Shannon Schlecht answered questions about a trademark battle during a Minnesota House Agriculture Finance and Policy Committee meeting Wednesday, Feb. 25.
items.summary:
AURI, a Minnesota non-profit organization, is seeking $78,000 from the state to cover legal fees incurred in a trademark dispute with a nutrition company called Auri Nutrition. 

Key details:
- AURI (the Agriculture Utilization and Research Institute) has received over 100 phone calls from consumers who mistakenly thought they were contacting Auri Nutrition, a similar-sounding company.
- The $78,000 request would help AURI protect its trademark and stop the other company from using their branding.
- AURI has been active in Minnesota since 1987, receiving state funding of over $4.5 million annually in fiscal years 2026 and 2027.
- The bill for the $78,000 appropriation is authored by co-chairs Rep. Paul Anderson (R-Starbuck) and Rep. Rick Hansen (DFL-South St. Paul).
- An expected decision on the trademark case would come in July 2026.
- AURI's executive director, Shannon Schlecht, says the organization hopes a positive ruling could help stop the other company from using their branding, as the confusion has already misdirected people seeking AURI's services.
- Rep. Bobbie Harder (R-Henderson) asked why AURI couldn't use its own reserves to cover the costs, but Schlecht said the AURI board approved the request in hopes of recouping the funds elsewhere rather than using money intended for programming.

The goal is to protect the AURI brand and the 35 years of state investment in the organization, ensuring it can continue providing services to the agriculture industry without being misdirected to a different company.

items.title: USDA selling its flagship South Building in Washington, relocating staff
items.description: The move to vacate and sell the massive but aging USDA building is part of a broader cost-cutting initiative at the department, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Wednesday.
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Agriculture is selling its flagship South Building office hub on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., and relocating employees to other locations across the country by the end of the year. The move is part of a broader cost-cutting initiative, with the building having $1.6 billion in delinquent maintenance costs and about 80% of its offices vacant. items.title: USDA seeks input to strengthen ag data amid confidence concerns
items.description: The United States Department of Agriculture announced a 45-day public request for information at the Agricultural Outlook Forum. The post USDA seeks input to strengthen ag data amid confidence concerns appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is seeking input from farmers and agricultural stakeholders to strengthen the integrity, transparency, and usefulness of its data products. This follows a massive revision to the U.S. corn acres, which has led to increased scrutiny over USDA data accuracy.

Key points:
- USDA agencies, including the Economic Research Service, National Agricultural Statistics Service, and Office of the Chief Economist, produce statistical reports that serve as benchmarks for the industry, such as the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates, Crop Production Reports, and the January and July Cattle inventories.
- After the revision to U.S. corn acres, USDA leaders acknowledge there is room for improvement in ensuring farmers, ranchers, and other users better understand the processes and methodology behind these data and statistics.
- USDA is seeking input through a 45-day Request for Information (RFI) on Opportunities, Challenges, and Emerging Areas in Statistical Data, Analysis, and Research. Preliminary analysis of the feedback will be discussed at the 2026 Spring Data Users Meeting on April 22, 2026.
- USDA Chief Economist Dr. Justin Benavidez emphasized that maintaining credibility with producers is critical, as USDA's data products have long been the gold standard in market reporting.
- The agency is also exploring options for improving harvested acreage estimates, most likely without more farmer surveys.

items.title: Not the end: Testing, support could help farmers navigate PFAS
items.description: PFAS contamination is a nightmare for farmers, but it doesn’t have to be the end of the road. In Maine, out of 111 farms where PFAS was detected, only six have had to close their doors. Why? The Pine Tree State devoted considerable money, time and resources to its PFAS problem. What can we learn from Maine's response in how to help farmers deal with PFAS when it's inevitably found on your farm? The post Not the end: Testing, support could help farmers navigate PFAS appeared first on Farm and Dai
items.summary:
PFAS are "forever chemicals" that have permeated much of the land, soil, and groundwater.

Key points:
- PFAS contamination was first discovered on a Maine farm in 2016, prompting the state to establish a $60 million PFAS Fund and testing program. Maine is now a national leader in addressing PFAS on farms.
- Experts say many farmers lack the resources to properly test for and address PFAS contamination. Without a relief and support system, finding PFAS could just end up putting farms out of business.
- In Maine, only 6 out of 111 farms with PFAS found in soil or water have gone out of business, thanks to state support. Experts say PFAS contamination "does not generally have to mean the end of the farm" with the right tools and assistance.
- PFAS contamination is often linked to the use of sewage sludge/biosolids as fertilizer, as PFAS tends to accumulate in these materials. Efforts are being made to develop technologies like gasification to destroy PFAS in biosolids.
- Lawmakers are being urged to provide financial relief and long-term support for PFAS-impacted farmers, shield them from liability, prevent further contamination, and invest in research and risk communication.

items.title: President Trump’s State of Union Defies U.S. Supreme Courts Tariffs Rule
items.description: Tariff authority clash sets stage for refund battles, 301 escalations, and new pricing pressures across agrochemical supply chains. The post President Trump’s State of Union Defies U.S. Supreme Courts Tariffs Rule appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
S. Supreme Court ruling on tariff authority. Key points:

- The Trump administration has imposed new tariffs on agrochemicals, defying a Supreme Court ruling that limits the President's ability to unilaterally raise tariffs.
- This sets the stage for potential refund battles, further escalation of Section 301 tariffs, and new pricing pressures across the agrochemical supply chain.
- The Supreme Court ruled in 2020 that the President's tariff authority under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 is limited, requiring Congressional approval for long-term tariffs.
- However, the Trump administration has continued to impose new tariffs, creating legal uncertainty and potential challenges for farmers and agribusinesses.
- Experts warn this could lead to refund battles, as companies may seek to recover tariff payments deemed unlawful under the Supreme Court ruling.
- There are also concerns the administration may further escalate Section 301 tariffs in response, driving up costs for farmers.
- Overall, the clash between the White House and the courts is creating pricing pressures and supply chain disruptions in the agrochemical industry.

items.title: Ag leaders talk farming outlook, uncertainty at town hall meeting in Barnesville
items.description: Around a dozen local residents attended a town hall meeting hosted by the Minnesota Farmers Union on Tuesday. The event was part of a series of meetings the organization is holding across Minnesota.
items.summary:
Summary:

Minnesota agricultural leaders warned of an impending farm crisis at a town hall meeting in Barnesville, Minnesota on February 24, 2026. Minnesota Farmers Union President Gary Wertish compared current economic conditions to the 1980s farm crisis, with farmers facing low prices and high input costs driven by Trump-era tariffs.

Minnesota Department of Agriculture Deputy Commissioner Andrea Vaubel acknowledged the challenges but said Minnesota has programs to support beginning farmers, provide downpayment assistance for farmland, and offer mental health specialists for farmers. However, she emphasized the need for federal policy changes on issues like climate and global trade.

Attendees raised concerns about workforce challenges, immigration reform, sustainable aviation fuel, and funding for programs that help schools purchase locally grown food. Clay County Commissioner Jenny Mongeau noted that federal and state policy changes have pushed costs down to local counties, putting a strain on farmers and landowners.

A unifying theme across the town halls was uncertainty, with Minnesota Farmers Union Vice President Anne Schwagerl highlighting rapid federal policy changes, often announced over social media, that affect farmers across the industry. The Minnesota Farmers Union plans to present a report of the discussions to elected officials.

items.title: Strategic Farming: Let's talk cover crops!
items.summary:
Researchers at the University of Minnesota examined planting cover crops, specifically winter cereal rye and a mix of annual cover crops, in corn-soybean and continuous corn rotations.

Key findings:
- In most years, the silage corn system without cover crops had the highest nitrate concentrations in tile drainage water.
- The winter cereal rye cover crop reduced nitrate concentrations in 3 out of 4 years, while the annual cover crop mix only reduced nitrates in 1 out of 4 years.
- Continuous corn harvested for grain had lower nitrate losses than silage corn in 3 out of 4 years.
- Successful cover crop establishment and growth is crucial for reducing nitrate losses, but this can be challenging in Minnesota.

The article also discusses cover crop management:
- Cover crops may fit better in shorter-season crops like peas, sweet corn, small grains, and corn silage which allow more time for establishment and growth.
- The most consistently successful cover crop in corn-soybean rotations is winter cereal rye.
- Research on different seeding rates (30-135 lbs/acre) and termination timings (10 days before, at, or 10 days after soybean planting) found no significant differences in cover crop biomass or soybean yields.

The University of Minnesota is hosting a "Cover Crop Academy" training program for crop advisors, consultants, and ag professionals to learn about cover crop management.

items.title: In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast
items.description: “The fishing industry has taken a lot of hits in the last few years, and most of them hit the small guys the hardest,” says Dixon. “We’re seeing more and more families not being able to afford to maintain a small commercial fishing vessel, leading to more large businesses taking over.” Dixon, a co-founder of […] The post In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast appeared first on Civil Eats.
items.summary:
The fishing industry in Oregon has faced significant challenges in recent years, with small-scale commercial fishermen struggling to maintain their businesses. As larger companies take over, many families are unable to afford to maintain small commercial fishing vessels.

To address this issue, a local seafood movement has emerged, led by organizations such as Catch It Coastal and the Cannon Beach Farmers Market. These initiatives work to promote locally-caught seafood and provide direct-to-consumer sales opportunities for small-scale fishermen.

The Cannon Beach Farmers Market, for example, has seen a significant increase in seafood sales, with 25% of total sales coming from seafood in 2021, up from 10% in previous years. This has provided a crucial outlet for local fishermen to sell their catch and connect with consumers.

The article highlights the story of fisherman Brock Dixon, who has benefited from the local seafood movement. Dixon says the movement has helped his business, allowing him to maintain his small commercial fishing vessel and continue providing high-quality seafood to local consumers.

Overall, the local seafood movement in Oregon is playing a vital role in supporting small-scale commercial fishermen and providing consumers with access to fresh, locally-sourced seafood. This trend has the potential to strengthen coastal communities and promote sustainable fishing practices.

items.title: High demand dwindles hay supplies as dry weather persists
items.description: Texas Crop and Weather Report - Feb. 24, 2026 The post High demand dwindles hay supplies as dry weather persists appeared first on AgriLife Today.
items.summary:
A bumper hay crop in 2025 initially provided a surplus, but that supply is now dwindling as livestock producers rely on it amid the ongoing dry weather.

- Hay supplies are tightening in drier areas, while other regions remain well-stocked. Round bale prices range from $75-$85 on average, with premium bales $110-$145.
- Rainfall deficits of 8 inches or more since September have severely impacted grazing and pasture recovery across central and west Texas. Some areas have received small amounts of rain, but more substantial precipitation is needed.
- The pasture mealybug, an invasive pest, is raising concerns among hay producers in South Texas if it continues to spread.
- The long-range forecast calls for above-normal temperatures and below-normal rainfall, further straining hay and grazing outlook.
- Livestock producers are heavily supplementing cattle diets with hay and feed as pasture conditions remain poor. Some have started shipping animals.
- Winter wheat is in poor to fair condition overall, with varying impacts from the dry weather depending on location. Warm-season forage production is also expected to be low.
- Texas A&M AgriLife Extension experts say a major rainfall event is needed across the state to help replenish soil moisture, pastures, and improve prospects for the upcoming growing season.

items.title: EPA Repeals Power Plant Regulations That Reduce Mercury in Fish

This action was announced on February 24, 2026 by EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, who cited an earlier version of the rule as being too burdensome for the industry. The repeal will likely lead to increased mercury levels in fish, posing greater health risks for farmers and their families who consume these fish. Experts warn that this decision could have significant negative impacts on agricultural communities and encourage the EPA to reconsider its position and reinstate the regulations to protect public health and the environment.

items.title: The 2025 growing season in Illinois: good but not great
items.description: The 2025 growing season in Illinois delivered another storyline characterized by sharp weather contrasts, average crop condition ratings, some disease pressure in places, and very good — if not record-setting — yields in many, but not all, areas. As we have seen before, crops showed their ability to translate good mid-season conditions to good yields even with very dry late-season conditions. A tale of two springs March was 4-5 degrees warmer and 2-3 inches drier than normal statewide,…
items.summary:
Overall, the state saw good to very good crop condition ratings and yields, though not record-breaking levels.

Key statistics:
- Corn yields averaged 214 bushels per acre, 3 bushels less than the 2024 record.
- Soybean yields averaged 62.5 bushels per acre, 1.5 bushels less than 2024.
- August and September were very dry, with only 3.1 inches of rain statewide.
- Corn kernel weights were lower than expected, averaging 85,000-90,000 kernels per bushel compared to 70,000-75,000 in previous drought years.
- Soybean seed size was small, with 3,000-3,600 seeds per pound compared to the usual 2,100-3,500.

Experts note that the good early-season conditions, including proper root development and canopy growth, allowed crops to withstand the late-season drought to some degree. However, areas that missed July rains saw reduced yields due to kernel/seed abortion and lower weights.

Recommendations for farmers include monitoring crop conditions closely and being prepared to adjust management practices based on weather patterns. Experts also suggest further research into improving crop resilience to variable weather.

items.title: AgriLife Extension publishes human, pet fact sheets on New World screwworm

The Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service has released two new fact sheets on the New World screwworm, a potentially devastating parasite that can infest humans, pets, livestock, and wildlife. 

The key information includes:

- New World screwworm poses a significant threat, and infestations can be fatal if left untreated. 
- As of January 2026, the U.S. has reported 1 travel-related human case.
- Risk factors for humans include traveling to regions where screwworm is present, working closely with livestock/wildlife, and having open wounds.
- Pets near the southern U.S. border and those traveling to/from Latin America are at highest risk. Veterinary advice is recommended for pre-travel treatment.
- Early detection is essential for effective treatment of pets.
- Protection tips include daily pet checks, assessing the pet environment, and monitoring for unusual behavior.
- There are no confirmed cases in Texas yet, but Texans are encouraged to report any suspected cases to healthcare providers, the Texas Animal Health Commission, or Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

The two new fact sheets, authored by AgriLife Extension experts, provide research-based information on risk factors, prevention, and reporting for both human health and companion animal care.

items.title: Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision
items.description: National farm groups reacted with relief after the Supreme Court rules against global tariffs, citing record-high supply costs. The post Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
S. Supreme Court struck down President Trump's global tariffs in a 6-3 ruling on February 20, 2026. Agricultural groups responded with cautious relief, stating the tariffs had hurt farmers who were already struggling with record-high input costs. 

The court ruled that the tariffs, which included a 10% "reciprocal" tariff on almost all countries, exceeded the powers given to the president by Congress. Trump had cited drug trafficking and trade deficits as national security threats to justify the tariffs, but the court said no president had used this law to impose tariffs "of this magnitude and scope."

In response, Trump announced a new 10% global tariff under a different law that allows him to impose tariffs for 150 days without congressional approval. He later said he'd raise this to 15%. 

Farm groups, including the American Soybean Association and National Association of Wheat Growers, urged Trump to back down on the tariffs, which have driven up the costs of critical farming inputs like fertilizer, seeds, and equipment. Soybean and wheat farmers in particular have been hit hard by "stubbornly high supply costs and low crop prices" over the past three years.

- Reach and frequency within target segments
- Engagement trends over time
- View-through conversions

S. but operate on a limited share of agricultural land. Nearly half of U.S. farms (around 50%) report less than $10,000 in annual sales, but these small operations account for only about 8% of total farmland nationwide.

items.title: 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February
items.description: Most farmers plant cover crops in the fall, and let the winter terminate them before they go to seed. But you can still plant cover crops in winter, as long as you know which will work in your climate. Plant these five cover crops this month for early spring benefits. The post 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Some cover crops to consider planting in February include:

Spinach - Spinach is a cold-season cover crop that can be sown densely now. Studies show it increases good bacteria and fungi in the soil, especially beneficial for plots where peppers will be planted later. Spinach needs soil temperatures of at least 40°F (4°C) to germinate.

Kale - Kale is a multipurpose cover crop that feeds the soil, provides greens for you and your customers, and can even be used as livestock feed. Kale needs slightly warmer soil of at least 45°F (7°C) to grow. Resistant varieties are recommended in disease-prone areas.

Daikon radish - Also called forage radishes, daikon have long taproots that reach deep into the soil to extract nutrients and break up compacted soil. They can be sown in February if the soil is at least 65°F (18°C).

Oats - Oats make a good cover crop, especially when combined with peas to fix nitrogen. Oats can tolerate temperatures down to 20°F (-7°C). Sow at a rate of 4-6 oz per 100 sq ft.

Buckwheat - Buckwheat is a quick-maturing cover crop that conditions poor soils and attracts pollinators. It can be used as a mulch after termination.

Planting these cover crops in February can improve soil health, increase subsequent crop yields, and provide economic benefits for farms. Experts recommend using low tunnels or other protection if the soil is still cold in your area.

items.title: Frosting Seeding Legumes
items.description: Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes, such as red clover, into a tired pasture or within a small grain stand. It is a potentially cost-effective solution to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes to an existing forage stand. Frost seeding is usually not recommended with grass species. The success of frost seeding hinges upon assessing the condition of the existing stand and seeding at the proper time.
items.summary:
Key Points:

1. Frost seeding involves broadcasting or overseeding legumes like red clover into a tired pasture or small grain stand to revitalize it. It is a cost-effective solution.

2. Timing is critical - typically between mid-February and early March, coinciding with the freeze-thaw cycle. The goal is to get the seed on bare soil.

3. The condition of the existing stand is important. A thick thatch can hinder seed-to-soil contact, so it's recommended to closely hay or overgraze in the fall/winter prior to frost seeding.

4. Soil type influences success - frost seeding tends to work better on loam or clay soils with sufficient moisture, as the freeze-thaw cycle helps incorporate the seed. Sandy or very dry soils are less ideal.

5. Adequate spring moisture is vital for establishing a healthy, frost-seeded stand. The potential benefits are high, but timing, soil condition, and moisture are key factors.

6. The article was written by Shelby Gruss, an assistant professor and forage extension specialist at Iowa State University, who joined the department in November 2023.

items.title: 7 Vegetables to Start From Seed in February

1. February is an ideal time to start growing various vegetable seeds indoors, even in cold climates, by using protected growing environments like greenhouses, cold frames, or low/high tunnels.

2. Vegetables recommended to start from seed in February include slow-growing herbs (basil, rosemary), tomatoes, peppers, brassicas (broccoli, cauliflower), lettuce, carrots, parsnips, and alliums (onions, leeks).

3. Tomatoes and peppers can take 80+ days from seed to fruit, so starting them in February allows for a head start and larger, healthier plants by the time spring arrives.

5. Alliums like onions and leeks should be started from seed in February to have mature transplants ready for spring planting.

6. Proper seed starting techniques are important, such as using heat mats, providing adequate lighting, and repotting seedlings as needed to prevent them from becoming root-bound.

7. Farmers in warmer regions may have more flexibility in their seed starting timelines, while those in colder climates need to account for potential late spring frosts when moving seedlings outdoors.

items.title: Evaluating soybean performance in conservation systems – project report
items.description: You can also read the article in Portuguese and Spanish Introduction Recent dust storm events in central Illinois and across the Midwest have renewed attention on soil conservation, especially after the tragic May 2023 event near Springfield that caused an 80-vehicle pileup, eight fatalities, and dozens of injuries. These incidents highlight that soil loss is not only an agronomic issue but also a public safety and environmental concern. Reduced tillage and cover crops are well-established pract
items.summary:
Field trials were conducted in 2024-2025 across 6 sites in central Illinois and north-central Iowa on productive soils.

The study evaluated 4 management systems: conventional tillage (CT), fall strip-tillage (ST), no-tillage (NT), and no-tillage with a cereal rye cover crop (NT+CR). Each system was paired with 3 starter fertilizer strategies: unfertilized control, 15 lb N/ac, and 15 lb N/ac + 10 lb S/ac.

Key findings:
- Starter fertilizer increased early-season soybean biomass by ~12% in Illinois, but did not persist to improve yields.
- Soybean yields ranged from 60-95 bu/ac across locations, with no significant yield differences between tillage/cover crop systems.
- On average, CT and ST yielded 78.4 bu/ac, NT 77.6 bu/ac, and NT+CR 76.2 bu/ac.
- When accounting for operational costs, NT had the highest partial net return, followed by ST and CT, while NT+CR had the lowest due to higher cover crop costs.

The project will continue in 2026 to track medium-term responses as soil, residue, and nutrient dynamics change under conservation systems. These findings are preliminary, with more data to be released upon completion.

Many farms are in a seasonal pause during this time due to winter weather, but greenhouses allow for continued production.

Greenhouses trap thermal heat to warm plants, with features like vents, frames, and climate control systems. Different types of greenhouses are discussed, including modular plastic greenhouses (can raise temps 30°F), low tunnels (2-15°F warmer), cold frames (5-15°F warmer), and designer greenhouses for year-round growing.

For February greenhouse planting, the article recommends:
- Tomatoes and peppers - Benefit from early indoor planting, need consistent 50°F+ temps.
- Brassicas (kale, cabbage, cauliflower, etc.) - Grow indoors to avoid pests and cold.
- Lettuces - Start early for spring harvest, protected from pests.
- Potatoes - Get a head start on full-sized spring potatoes.
- Onions - Start seed onions, chives, garlic chives.
- Flowers - Start long-germination flowers like lisianthus, coneflower, dahlias.

The article notes the importance of considering the specific greenhouse setup when choosing what to grow. It provides tips on climate control, lighting, and planting methods for greenhouse growing.

items.title: Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land
items.description: Also called agroforestry, forest farming is a great way to work within your environmental parameters and utilize the tree canopy to produce more for your farm. Especially for those who live in forested areas, this practice enhances farm output without compromising the ecosystem. The post Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Originating in Brazil's tropical rainforests, this practice allows for diverse, self-sustaining agricultural systems that work within local ecological bounds.

The most common forest farming method is thinning a forest to create optimal growing conditions for crops in the understory. Suitable crops range from native ornamentals to fungi, fruit, timber, and forest food crops. Other approaches include silvopasture (combining forestry and ranching) and alley cropping (planting specialty crops between rows of trees).

Forest farming offers numerous benefits:
- Improved water and soil quality, with tree roots holding water and recharging groundwater 
- Carbon sequestration, storing up to 22 lbs of carbon per year in the first 20 years
- Enhanced biodiversity, as trees host a variety of beneficial insects, birds, mammals, fungi, and bacteria
- Opportunities to grow specialized crops like mushrooms, ramps, syrups, and edible roots

Lands with existing forests or riparian areas are well-suited for forest farming. Farmers should consult local agricultural extension offices to develop a forest management plan and identify compatible crops for their market. There are also regulations to consider around wild plant species.

Overall, forest farming can be an inexpensive way for farmers to diversify their operations and gain both financial and ecological benefits from their forested land.

items.title: Getting Started with Spray Drones in Iowa: A Practical Guide

items.summary:
Defining Objectives: Spray drones can provide flexibility for timely applications, reduce field traffic, and access hard-to-reach areas. Farmers should identify their specific challenges to determine if drone use, hiring a custom operator, or cooperating with neighbors is best.

2. Regulatory Requirements: Operators must have an FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate, FAA Part 137 Certification for aerial pesticide application, and appropriate Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship (IDALS) licensing. Only products labeled for aerial use can be applied by drone.

3. Insurance and Risk Management: Farmers need specific coverage for chemical liability, general liability, and drone/equipment damage. Consulting an insurance provider is essential.

4. Equipment Selection: Factors like spray tank capacity, battery life, nozzle options, and GPS capabilities should be considered when choosing a drone system. Demonstrations can help new users.

5. Training and Safe Operation: Proper training on flight, calibration, weather monitoring, and maintenance is critical for effective and responsible drone use.

6. Gradual Adoption: The article recommends starting with small acreage trials to develop efficient procedures before expanding drone use. Dry product applications like cover crop seeding can also be evaluated cautiously.

7. Iowa Resources: Iowa State University, the Digital Ag Innovation Lab, dealers, and IDALS can provide support and guidance for Iowa farmers adopting spray drone technology.

8. Future Developments: Ongoing improvements in payload, automation, and precision integration will shape the long-term role of spray drones in Iowa agriculture.

items.title: The 9 Best Flowers and Vegetables to Winter Sow
items.description: For farms in colder areas, starting seeds in time for the spring market requires a significant amount of time and indoor space. The post The 9 Best Flowers and Vegetables to Winter Sow appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Comprehensive Summary:

Farmers can maximize profits and productivity by winter sowing hardy annuals and perennials. This method involves starting seeds in containers like milk jugs or plastic bags, placed outdoors to take advantage of cold, moist conditions that help break seed dormancy. This results in hardier transplants that mature faster.

The best vegetables to winter sow include:
- Cabbages - Choose standard, Napa, or fast-maturing 'Carex' types
- Spinach - 'Avon' is mildew/blight resistant; 'Space' resists bolting
- Onions - Match day length to your latitude (long, short, or intermediate-day) 
- Leafy greens like kale, collards, chard, watercress, and microgreens

Good flowers for winter sowing include perennials like pansies, echinacea, snapdragons, larkspur, and scabiosa. These provide pest control and cut flowers.

Planting these hardy crops and flowers now allows them to get a head start, leading to earlier harvests and blooms come spring.

items.title: Farmer sentiment improves despite financial performance concerns
items.description: Three broad-based measures of farmer sentiment improved in July as the Purdue University/CME Group Ag Economy Barometer index rose 8 points to 113, the Index of Current Conditions increased by 10 points to 100, and the Index of Future Expectations at 119 was 7 points higher than a month earlier. Despite declines in corn and soybean prices from mid-June to mid-July — Eastern Corn Belt cash prices fell 11% and 5%, respectively — farmer sentiment improved in July. Responses to the individual questi
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Farmer sentiment improved in July 2024, with the Purdue/CME Group Ag Economy Barometer index rising 8 points to 113.

- The Index of Current Conditions increased by 10 points to 100, and the Index of Future Expectations rose 7 points to 119.

- This positive shift was attributed to fewer respondents reporting worsened conditions compared to a year ago and a decrease in those expecting negative future outcomes.

- High input costs remained the biggest concern for 34% of farmers, while 29% cited the risk of lower crop and livestock prices as a top concern, up from 25% in June.

- Despite concerns about financial performance, the Farm Capital Investment Index rose 6 points in July to 38, though it remains 7 points lower than in July 2023.

- The Short-Term Farmland Value Expectations Index improved slightly, while the Long-Term Farmland Value Expectations Index dropped 6 points.

- Nearly three-fourths (72%) of crop farmer respondents expect cash rental rates to remain roughly the same as in 2024, with the remaining respondents evenly divided between expecting a rise or a decline in rates.

items.title: Purdue researchers adopt interdisciplinary approach to assessing emerging tar spot disease in corn
items.description: For more than a century, tar spot fungal disease in corn kept its distance from the U.S., biding its time
items.summary:
Purdue researchers are taking an interdisciplinary approach to assess the emerging tar spot disease in corn:

- Tar spot fungal disease in corn had not been detected in the U.S. until 2015, but has been endemic in several Latin American countries since 1904.
- The disease has now spread to 16 U.S. states and Ontario, Canada by 2022, affecting crops in 15 other countries as well.
- Purdue researchers, led by C.D. Cruz, are applying a mix of statistical, data science, epidemiology, microbiology, AI, and computer vision methods to better understand the dynamics of tar spot.
- Their work is funded by two USDA grants totaling nearly $1.1 million.
- Collaborators include researchers from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador, South Korea, and the U.S.
- Previous work by the team has included developing a digital method to quantify tar spot using an algorithm called SCDA, with some inaccuracies still being refined.
- The team is also integrating drone imagery, weather data, and AI approaches with traditional statistical methods to capture details about the tar spot pathosystem.
- The interdisciplinary nature of the project can place greater time demands, but also leads to better problem-solving by leveraging each researcher's expertise.
- The overall goal is to quantify and model tar spot severity to provide rapid and accurate information to stakeholders and address biosecurity challenges.

items.title: Wisconsin Winter Wheat Update
items.description: Damon Smith, Extension Field Crops Pathologist, Shawn Conley, Extension Soybean and Small Grains Agronomist, University of Wisconsin-Madison Winter wheat in Wisconsin continues to move through growth stages at record pace. We are about 10-14 days …
items.summary:
Wisconsin winter wheat is progressing faster than usual, about 10-14 days ahead of the normal schedule. As of April 21st, 90% of the crop has reached the Feekes 5 growth stage (leaf sheath strongly erected) compared to the 5-year average of 70% at this time.

Crop conditions are generally good, with 75% of the crop rated in good or excellent condition, compared to 68% last year. However, some areas have experienced winterkill, with estimates of 10-20% crop loss in the southern and central parts of the state. 

Nitrogen application is recommended when the crop reaches Feekes 5 to optimize yield. Farmers are advised to scout fields closely for diseases like Fusarium head blight, which can significantly reduce yields. The economic threshold for fungicide application is 20% of heads showing symptoms.

Shawn Conley, Extension Soybean and Small Grains Agronomist at UW-Madison, states "Given the accelerated crop development, growers should be prepared to time nitrogen and fungicide applications appropriately to maximize yield potential."

items.title: Questions to consider prior to replanting a soybean field
items.description: Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist, UW-Madison Early in the growing season, abiotic (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding, etc.) and biotic (slugs, deer, disease, insects, etc.) factors often reduce soybean plant stands. A soybean …
items.summary:
Key points:

- Abiotic factors like freezing temperatures, hail, and flooding, as well as biotic factors like slugs, deer, disease, and insects, can reduce soybean plant stands early in the season.
- Replanting soybeans may be an option, but there are several questions farmers should consider first:
  - What was the initial soybean planting date?
  - How much of the field needs to be replanted?
  - What is the soybean seed availability and cost?
  - What are the yield implications of replanting later in the season?
  - Will the replanted soybeans compete with the remaining plants?
- Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist at UW-Madison, recommends carefully evaluating these factors before deciding to replant, as it may not always be the best option.
- Replanting too late can result in significantly reduced yields compared to the initial planting.
- Farmers should work with agronomists and extension specialists to make the best decision for their operation.

items.summary:
The University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension warns that farmers planning to use 2,4-D for post-emergence weed control in Enlist E3 soybeans may face restrictions starting in 2024. 

Key points:
- The 2,4-D herbicide is currently approved for use on Enlist E3 soybeans, but this approval is set to expire on December 20, 2023.
- The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is currently reviewing whether to renew the 2,4-D registration for use on Enlist E3 soybeans beyond 2023.
- If the 2,4-D registration is not renewed, farmers will no longer be able to use 2,4-D for post-emergence weed control in Enlist E3 soybeans after December 20, 2023.
- Farmers are advised to plan ahead and consider alternative weed management strategies in case the 2,4-D registration is not renewed.
- Rodrigo Werle, Weed Scientist and Extension Specialist at UW-Madison, recommends that farmers consult with their local Extension office to stay updated on the 2,4-D registration status and explore alternative weed control options.
